screens.title: Routine Maintenance Tasks
screens.narratorSegment: Routine maintenance is the set of scheduled activities that keep a MySQL server healthy, performant, and safe. In production you'll balance table maintenance like collecting statistics and reclaiming space, careful log retention to avoid disk exhaustion, integrity checks for corrupted tables, routine security audits of accounts and privileges, and automation so those tasks run reliably. This lesson will give you practical commands, safety checks, and scheduling patterns you can adopt. For example, when a table has many deletes, rebuilding or optimizing can reclaim space but may lock the table; when you need fresh index statistics after a large import, analyze is faster and less intrusive. For logs, binary logs are essential for replication and recovery but must be expired or purged safely so they do not fill disk. You will also see how to schedule purges using the Event Scheduler and how to review grants regularly. By the end you should understand which commands to run, when they are safe, and how to automate them so routine maintenance becomes predictable and low risk.

screens.title: What is Routine Maintenance?
screens.narratorSegment: Routine maintenance is a regular set of operations performed to keep a database available, performant, and secure. Think of it like vehicle maintenance: oil changes and inspections at set intervals prevent bigger failures later. In MySQL, maintenance includes table optimization and statistics collection, log management to avoid disk exhaustion, integrity checks and repairs where appropriate, regular security audits of user accounts and privileges, and automated tasks to make these actions repeatable. Scope and frequency depend on activity: a high-write system needs more frequent analysis and space reclamation; a lightly updated archive may need less. Planning means deciding which tasks run daily, weekly, or monthly, who owns them, and how you verify completion. For example, daily tasks often include rotating error and slow query logs and checking available disk space. Weekly tasks might include running ANALYZE TABLE after large imports, and monthly tasks might include OPTIMIZE TABLE on highly fragmented tables. A common misconception is that running expensive tasks as often as possible is always better; in reality, some commands lock tables or are resource intensive and require scheduling in low-traffic windows or using online alternatives. Before running any maintenance, always consider backups and the impact on replication or availability. What small, repeatable routine will you add this week to reduce risk?

Module 08 › Chapter 8.6 › What is Routine Maintenance?
Definition & planning
Regular operations to preserve performance, integrity, and security.
  • Define a cadence: daily checks, weekly refreshes, monthly reclamation.
  • Assign ownership and verification steps to prevent drift.
  • Balance impact: avoid running heavy tasks during peak traffic.
  • Automate repeatable tasks and keep critical decisions manual with review.
Analogy
Like scheduled car service: small, routine checks prevent big failures.
Common mistake
Running expensive operations without maintenance windows or backups.
Recommended cadence example
Daily
Rotate logs, check disk usage, review error log entries and slow query summaries.
Weekly
Run ANALYZE TABLE after imports or large modifications to refresh optimizer statistics.
Monthly
Consider OPTIMIZE TABLE on heavily fragmented tables during maintenance windows; review user privileges.
Key Takeaway
Key Takeaway

Schedule tasks by impact and duration. Automate safe tasks and reserve heavy operations for maintenance windows.

screens.title: OPTIMIZE TABLE explained
screens.narratorSegment: OPTIMIZE TABLE rebuilds a table and its indexes, reclaiming space left behind by deletes and updates and refreshing index structures. For InnoDB this is effectively a rebuild: MySQL creates a temporary copy, copies data, then swaps the table. That makes OPTIMIZE very effective after heavy deletions but also resource intensive and potentially locking. In production, you must consider availability: running OPTIMIZE on a large table can block queries or stress disk and input and output. A safer pattern is to perform OPTIMIZE during a maintenance window or use online tools such as pt-online-schema-change in environments where table locks are unacceptable. A common misconception is that OPTIMIZE is always necessary after any delete; in many cases ANALYZE TABLE is enough to refresh statistics for the optimizer without a rebuild. As a concrete example, if an orders table had 30% of rows deleted after archiving old orders, running OPTIMIZE TABLE orders could reclaim disk space and compact indexes. Before you run it, ensure you have recent backups and, if using replication, verify slaves are not relying on binary logs you plan to purge. If you cannot schedule downtime, plan an online approach instead. How would you balance reclamation with availability in your environment?

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.6 › OPTIMIZE TABLE explained
OPTIMIZE TABLE
Rebuilds a table to defragment data and reclaim space.
OPTIMIZE TABLE my_database.my_table;
• It performs a rebuild for InnoDB, which may create a temporary copy.
• It reclaims space and rebuilds indexes, which can improve I/O and storage efficiency.
• It can be resource intensive and may lock tables; schedule during low traffic or use online alternatives.
Safety note
Have backups and a maintenance window. Consider pt-online-schema-change for online rebuilds.
Example scenario
If a high-traffic table used for orders had heavy deletes after an archive, fragmentation can make scans slower. Opting to rebuild that table once per month during a maintenance window can reclaim space and reduce I/O. If you cannot accept downtime, coordinate an online schema change or move data to a new table in small batches.
Common mistake
Assuming OPTIMIZE always speeds queries. Sometimes updating statistics with ANALYZE TABLE is sufficient and much faster.
Key Takeaway

Use OPTIMIZE to reclaim space after heavy churn, but plan for its cost and lock behavior. Prefer online tools for production with high availability needs.

screens.title: ANALYZE TABLE vs OPTIMIZE TABLE
screens.narratorSegment: ANALYZE TABLE and OPTIMIZE TABLE serve different maintenance goals and have different costs. ANALYZE TABLE gathers key distribution statistics about the table and its indexes so the optimizer can pick better execution plans. It is relatively fast and non-intrusive, and you should run it after large imports, mass deletes, or major updates to ensure the optimizer has accurate information. OPTIMIZE TABLE is a rebuild operation that defragments data and indexes and reclaims space. It is more disruptive and more time-consuming. A concrete example: after importing a multi-million-row CSV into a reporting table, ANALYZE TABLE will update statistics quickly so queries choose appropriate indexes. Later, after a batch archival that removed a large percentage of rows, OPTIMIZE TABLE may be appropriate to shrink storage and reduce table bloat. A common misconception is to use OPTIMIZE whenever queries are slow. Often, stale statistics are the cause and ANALYZE TABLE provides a fast fix. Remember to measure effects with EXPLAIN before and after, and schedule OPTIMIZE carefully. Which approach will you pick when a table’s query plans change after a data load? ANALYZE TABLE vs OPTIMIZE TABLE means analyze updates optimizer statistics quickly; optimize rebuilds storage to reclaim space. use analyze for stats, optimize for fragmentation.. In practical terms, when to update statistics and when to rebuild. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.6 › ANALYZE TABLE vs OPTIMIZE TABLE
ANALYZE TABLE
Collects index distribution statistics used by the optimizer.
ANALYZE TABLE my_database.my_table;
  • Fast and less intrusive than optimize.
  • Useful immediately after large imports, deletes, or updates.
  • Helps the optimizer choose better plans without rebuilding storage.
When to use
After major data changes that affect index selectivity.
OPTIMIZE TABLE
Rebuilds table to defragment and reclaim space.
OPTIMIZE TABLE my_database.my_table;
  • Resource intensive and may lock the table for its duration.
  • Reclaims disk space and compacts indexes after heavy deletes or updates.
  • Prefer running under maintenance windows or via online alternatives.
When to use
When physical fragmentation significantly affects storage and I/O and you can accept the cost.
Checklist before you run
Verify backups are current.
Check replication slaves for required binary logs.
Schedule during low-traffic windows.

screens.title: Log File Management
screens.narratorSegment: Log files are critical to operations and can be a source of disk exhaustion if not managed. MySQL produces binary logs for replication and point-in-time recovery, the error log for server messages, the slow query log to find inefficient queries, and rarely the general query log which records everything. Each log type has a different purpose and retention requirement. For binary logs, set expire_logs_days to keep only the number of days you need for replication and recovery. For error and slow logs, use system-level rotation such as logrotate to rotate files and prevent growth. A safe retention strategy starts with identifying the recovery and replication needs: how many days of binary logs do you need to replay for point-in-time recovery, and do your slaves require older files? Then configure expire_logs_days and a rotation policy for the other logs. A common mistake is purging binary logs without checking slave replication positions; always verify slave status before deleting logs needed by replication. Automating log purges and rotation reduces human error and ensures logs do not silently fill disk space. Log File Management means treat each log type differently: retain binary logs for recovery/replication and rotate other logs to control disk usage.. In practical terms, types of logs and a safe retention strategy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.6 › Log File Management
Log types
Binary Log (log_bin)
Used for replication and point-in-time recovery. Can grow large and must be purged carefully.
Error Log (log_error)
Contains server messages and errors. Rotate regularly and inspect for recurring issues.
Slow Query Log
Helps identify inefficient queries and should be rotated to avoid disk bloat.
General Query Log
High overhead; rarely enabled in production. If enabled, rotate strictly.
Retention pattern
Decide retention based on replication and recovery needs. Configure automatic expiry for binary logs and use system rotation for other logs.
Checklist before purge
  • • Confirm no slave requires the logs you intend to remove.
  • • Verify backups and point-in-time recovery windows.
  • • Automate retention rules to avoid manual mistakes.
Quick config
Set binary log expiry in my.cnf for automatic purging.
# my.cnf example
expire_logs_days = 7
Common mistake
Purging binary logs without checking slave replication positions; always verify slave status first.
Key Takeaway

Adopt retention policies that match your recovery needs and automate them so logs never silently exhaust disk space.

screens.title: Binary Logs: Purging Safely
screens.narratorSegment: Binary logs are essential for replication and point-in-time recovery, but if left unmanaged they grow indefinitely and risk filling disk. To manage them safely, first determine retention needs and the state of slaves. A safe manual purge example removes logs up to a named file or before a date. For example, PURGE BINARY LOGS TO 'mysql-bin.000123'; deletes all binary logs up to that file. Alternatively, PURGE BINARY LOGS BEFORE 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS'; removes older logs. Important safety checks: on each slave run SHOW SLAVE STATUS and note Master_Log_File and Exec_Master_Log_Pos to confirm they aren't behind the file you will remove. Another safe pattern is configuring expire_logs_days in my. cnf to let the server expire logs automatically. Automate purges only after confirming slaves and backups. A common misconception is that purging is harmless; purging logs used by a slave will break replication and may require expensive recovery. After purging, validate by running SHOW BINARY LOGS and confirming expected files remain. Which verification step will you add to your purge routine? Binary Logs: Purging Safely means always check slave positions and backups before purging binary logs; prefer automated expiry configured to your recovery window.. In practical terms, commands, safety checks, and replication considerations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.6 › Binary Logs: Purging Safely
Manual purge commands
Two common purge forms for immediate relief.
-- Purge up to a specific file
PURGE BINARY LOGS TO 'mysql-bin.000123';

-- Purge before a specific date/time
PURGE BINARY LOGS BEFORE '2023-01-01 00:00:00';
After purging, run SHOW BINARY LOGS to confirm which files remain. If slaves still require older logs, do not purge them. Automation is safer when combined with replication checks and backups.
Safety checklist
  • • Check each slave: SHOW SLAVE STATUS\G and inspect Master_Log_File and Exec_Master_Log_Pos.
  • • Ensure backups allow point-in-time recovery for the retention window.
  • • Prefer expire_logs_days for automated expiry aligned to your retention policy.
Common mistake
Purging logs required by slaves or forgetting to verify backups before deleting logs used for recovery.
Key Takeaway

Purge binary logs only after verifying replication and backups; prefer automatic expiry configured to your recovery window.

screens.title: Error, Slow, and General Logs
screens.narratorSegment: Error and slow query logs are valuable diagnostic tools but require rotation and regular inspection. The error log contains server-level messages such as startup errors, crashes, or plugin failures; check it periodically for recurring warnings that indicate emerging problems. The slow query log records queries that exceed a threshold; rotate it and inspect its contents to prioritize indexing or query refactoring. The general log captures all statements and is high overhead, so avoid enabling it in production except for short troubleshooting windows. Use system-level rotation tools like logrotate on Linux to archive and compress old logs and prevent growth. A practical pattern is to rotate logs daily and keep a short archive based on your operational needs. When you inspect logs, look for repeated patterns: the same error appearing frequently may point to a misconfiguration or failing job; repeated slow queries on particular tables indicate missing or poor indexes. A common misconception is to ignore slow logs because they grow quickly; instead automate rotation and use aggregated slow log summaries for periodic reviews. What log entry pattern would prompt you to open a troubleshooting ticket?

Module 08 › Chapter 8.6 › Error, Slow, and General Logs
Rotate logs
Use logrotate or similar to archive and compress logs and keep file sizes manageable.
• Rotate daily for busy servers or weekly for quieter systems.
• Compress older logs and keep a retention window aligned with troubleshooting needs.
• Avoid enabling general log in production; use it briefly for troubleshooting and then disable it.
Inspecting logs
Search for repeated errors, slow queries affecting the same tables, and signs of resource exhaustion.
Interpretation tips
  • • Multiple identical error entries usually indicate a systemic issue that needs configuration or code fixes.
  • • Slow query patterns linked to specific tables or joins suggest missing or ineffective indexes.
  • • Correlate log times with system metrics to find resource-related problems like spikes in I/O or memory.
Key Takeaway

Rotate logs and review them regularly. Automate rotation and keep a short archive so logs help troubleshooting without risking disk space.

screens.title: CHECK TABLE and REPAIR TABLE
screens.narratorSegment: CHECK TABLE verifies a table's integrity and reports problems; REPAIR TABLE attempts to fix corrupted MyISAM tables. For InnoDB, corruption is much rarer thanks to crash recovery and transaction logs; if an InnoDB table is corrupted, the safest response is usually a full restore from backup. Use CHECK TABLE on MyISAM when you suspect corruption or after an improper shutdown, and follow with REPAIR TABLE if necessary. Example commands are simple: CHECK TABLE my_database. my_table; and REPAIR TABLE my_database. my_table;. However, REPAIR TABLE may not be effective for InnoDB and can risk data loss if run without a backup. A misconception is to run REPAIR TABLE on any error; instead, interpret CHECK TABLE output carefully and prefer restoring InnoDB data from backups. Also consider exporting data to a new table if repair attempts are risky. Always ensure a recent backup before running repair operations and, when possible, test repair steps in a staging environment. If you maintain mixed engines, prioritize migrating critical tables to InnoDB to leverage its crash recovery features. CHECK TABLE and REPAIR TABLE means use check and repair for myisam; prefer backups and restores for innodb corruption, testing repair steps in staging first.. In practical terms, integrity checks, repair operations, and innodb considerations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 08 › Chapter 8.6 › CHECK & REPAIR TABLE
Integrity commands
CHECK TABLE my_database.my_table;
REPAIR TABLE my_database.my_table;
• CHECK TABLE reports corruption or structural problems.
• REPAIR TABLE attempts to fix MyISAM tables; not recommended for InnoDB.
• For InnoDB corruption, prefer restore from backup and evaluate causes.
Practical guidance
Always take a backup before repair actions. If possible test repair flow on a copy in staging. If REPAIR succeeds, validate data integrity and run ANALYZE to refresh statistics.
Common misconception
Assuming REPAIR is safe for all storage engines. InnoDB requires different recovery approaches.

Use check and repair appropriately by engine. For InnoDB, rely on backups and crash recovery; for MyISAM use repair carefully with backups and tests.

screens.title: Security Audits and Privilege Reviews
screens.narratorSegment: Security audits are routine checks of user accounts, privileges, authentication methods, and server configuration. Start by listing user accounts from mysql. user and inspect the grants for each account to ensure least privilege. Commands useful in this review include selecting user rows and SHOW GRANTS FOR 'user'@'host'; to see assigned privileges. Remove unused accounts and revoke privileges that are unnecessary. Also verify password strength and authentication plugins in use. A frequent misconception is to treat privileges as static; application needs change and privileges creep over time. Schedule regular reviews, and combine automated scans that report overly broad grants with human review before changes. When you remove an account or revoke privileges, ensure you log the change and test dependent applications in a staging environment if possible. Keep MySQL itself patched to reduce exposure to known vulnerabilities. Regular audits lower your exposure and make incident response simpler when an account is compromised. Which account would you audit first on a new server? Security Audits and Privilege Reviews means regularly remove unused accounts and revoke unnecessary privileges to reduce attack surface and simplify incident response.. In practical terms, regularly review accounts, grants, and credentials. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Audit steps
  • • List user accounts and inspect authentication methods.
  • • Use SHOW GRANTS FOR 'user'@'host'; to view privileges.
  • • Remove or disable unused accounts and revoke unnecessary rights.

SELECT user, host, authentication_string FROM mysql.user;
SHOW GRANTS FOR 'app_user'@'10.0.1.5';
Best practices
• Apply least privilege and role-based grants where possible.
• Schedule audits on a regular cadence and after team changes.
• Log privilege changes and test critical applications after revocation.
Common mistake
Leaving broad grants like ALL PRIVILEGES for convenience; this increases risk when accounts are compromised.

screens.title: Automation: cron and Event Scheduler
screens.narratorSegment: Automation ensures routine tasks run consistently and reduces human error. Two common automation methods are system cron jobs and MySQL's Event Scheduler. Use cron for shell scripts that can rotate logs, call mysql client to run commands, or manage backups. The Event Scheduler runs S Q L tasks inside MySQL itself and is convenient for database-only tasks. The chapter provides an Event example to purge binary logs daily: create an event that runs PURGE BINARY LOGS BEFORE (NOW() - INTERVAL 7 DAY) once per day. Remember to enable the scheduler with SET GLOBAL event_scheduler = ON; before creating events. When automating, include verification steps in scripts: check slave positions before purging binary logs, log actions and results to an audit table or file, and send alerts on failures. A misconception is to automate without retry and alerting; if a cron job silently fails you will miss critical maintenance. Test automation in a staging environment, and add safety checks that abort actions when preconditions are not met. Which maintenance task will you automate first and how will you verify its success?

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.6 › Automation: cron and Event Scheduler
Event Scheduler example
Enable the scheduler, then create a daily event that purges binary logs older than seven days.
-- Enable scheduler
SET GLOBAL event_scheduler = ON;

CREATE EVENT IF NOT EXISTS purge_old_binary_logs
ON SCHEDULE EVERY 1 DAY
STARTS CURRENT_TIMESTAMP + INTERVAL 1 HOUR
DO
    PURGE BINARY LOGS BEFORE (NOW() - INTERVAL 7 DAY);
Include verification steps in event logic where possible or have a secondary job that confirms the action completed successfully.
Cron approach
Use cron to run shell scripts that call mysql client, rotate logs, or back up databases, with built-in error handling and alerts.
Always test automation in staging and add logging and alerting so failures are visible and actionable.
Key Takeaway
Automate repeatable, safe tasks and include verification so automation reduces human overhead while preserving safety.

Step-by-step terminal demo
1) Configure expiry

# Restart MySQL then verify

2) Generate logs and inspect
USE test_db;
INSERT INTO products (id, name) VALUES (3, 'Monitor');
UPDATE products SET name = 'Gaming Monitor' WHERE id = 3;
DELETE FROM products WHERE id = 1;

3) Simulate purge
-- Verify slaves before running
-- Then run a purge (simulated)

ANALYZE TABLE troubleshooting_db.users;
OPTIMIZE TABLE troubleshooting_db.users;

Practice the verification steps first. Observe outputs and measure impact before automating or scheduling the operation in production.

fullNarratorScript:
Routine maintenance is the set of scheduled activities that keep a MySQL server healthy, performant, and safe. In production you'll balance table maintenance like collecting statistics and reclaiming space, careful log retention to avoid disk exhaustion, integrity checks for corrupted tables, routine security audits of accounts and privileges, and automation so those tasks run reliably. This lesson will give you practical commands, safety checks, and scheduling patterns you can adopt. For example, when a table has many deletes, rebuilding or optimizing can reclaim space but may lock the table; when you need fresh index statistics after a large import, analyze is faster and less intrusive. For logs, binary logs are essential for replication and recovery but must be expired or purged safely so they do not fill disk. You will also see how to schedule purges using the Event Scheduler and how to review grants regularly. By the end you should understand which commands to run, when they are safe, and how to automate them so routine maintenance becomes predictable and low risk.

Over the next screens you will gain practical skills to perform routine MySQL maintenance with confidence. First, you will identify which tasks are essential to keep MySQL healthy and how to prioritize them by risk and impact. That means learning to spot when a table needs maintenance or when logs threaten disk space. Second, you will learn the difference between OPTIMIZE TABLE and ANALYZE TABLE, including what each command changes, how intrusive they are, and when to prefer the faster, safer analyze. Third, you will manage log files: configure automatic expiration, inspect binary logs, and perform safe purges without breaking replication or recovery. Finally, you'll schedule and automate recurring work using cron or the MySQL Event Scheduler so routine tasks run reliably. Each skill includes a short verification milestone so you can confirm you performed the operation correctly in a controlled environment. These objectives focus on practical, repeatable actions you will use in production.

These next objectives complete the practical abilities you need to maintain a MySQL instance. Fifth, you'll be able to run CHECK TABLE and REPAIR TABLE and understand when they're appropriate, remembering that InnoDB's crash recovery makes corruption rarer while MyISAM still benefits from repair operations. Sixth, you'll perform regular security audits by listing user accounts, viewing grants, removing unused accounts, and revoking unnecessary privileges to reduce attack surface. Seventh, you'll learn to inspect error, slow, and general logs, set up rotation, and interpret entries that indicate instability or inefficient queries. Eighth, you'll plan a maintenance schedule combining quick daily tasks like log rotation and slower weekly or monthly tasks like optimize on tables with heavy fragmentation. Each card includes a small visual mnemonic and a verified milestone so you can demonstrate competence in a lab environment.

Routine maintenance is a regular set of operations performed to keep a database available, performant, and secure. Think of it like vehicle maintenance: oil changes and inspections at set intervals prevent bigger failures later. In MySQL, maintenance includes table optimization and statistics collection, log management to avoid disk exhaustion, integrity checks and repairs where appropriate, regular security audits of user accounts and privileges, and automated tasks to make these actions repeatable. Scope and frequency depend on activity: a high-write system needs more frequent analysis and space reclamation; a lightly updated archive may need less. Planning means deciding which tasks run daily, weekly, or monthly, who owns them, and how you verify completion. For example, daily tasks often include rotating error and slow query logs and checking available disk space. Weekly tasks might include running ANALYZE TABLE after large imports, and monthly tasks might include OPTIMIZE TABLE on highly fragmented tables. A common misconception is that running expensive tasks as often as possible is always better; in reality, some commands lock tables or are resource intensive and require scheduling in low-traffic windows or using online alternatives. Before running any maintenance, always consider backups and the impact on replication or availability. What small, repeatable routine will you add this week to reduce risk?

OPTIMIZE TABLE rebuilds a table and its indexes, reclaiming space left behind by deletes and updates and refreshing index structures. For InnoDB this is effectively a rebuild: MySQL creates a temporary copy, copies data, then swaps the table. That makes OPTIMIZE very effective after heavy deletions but also resource intensive and potentially locking. In production, you must consider availability: running OPTIMIZE on a large table can block queries or stress disk and input and output. A safer pattern is to perform OPTIMIZE during a maintenance window or use online tools such as pt-online-schema-change in environments where table locks are unacceptable. A common misconception is that OPTIMIZE is always necessary after any delete; in many cases ANALYZE TABLE is enough to refresh statistics for the optimizer without a rebuild. As a concrete example, if an orders table had 30% of rows deleted after archiving old orders, running OPTIMIZE TABLE orders could reclaim disk space and compact indexes. Before you run it, ensure you have recent backups and, if using replication, verify slaves are not relying on binary logs you plan to purge. If you cannot schedule downtime, plan an online approach instead. How would you balance reclamation with availability in your environment?

ANALYZE TABLE and OPTIMIZE TABLE serve different maintenance goals and have different costs. ANALYZE TABLE gathers key distribution statistics about the table and its indexes so the optimizer can pick better execution plans. It is relatively fast and non-intrusive, and you should run it after large imports, mass deletes, or major updates to ensure the optimizer has accurate information. OPTIMIZE TABLE is a rebuild operation that defragments data and indexes and reclaims space. It is more disruptive and more time-consuming. A concrete example: after importing a multi-million-row CSV into a reporting table, ANALYZE TABLE will update statistics quickly so queries choose appropriate indexes. Later, after a batch archival that removed a large percentage of rows, OPTIMIZE TABLE may be appropriate to shrink storage and reduce table bloat. A common misconception is to use OPTIMIZE whenever queries are slow. Often, stale statistics are the cause and ANALYZE TABLE provides a fast fix. Remember to measure effects with EXPLAIN before and after, and schedule OPTIMIZE carefully. Which approach will you pick when a table’s query plans change after a data load? ANALYZE TABLE vs OPTIMIZE TABLE means analyze updates optimizer statistics quickly; optimize rebuilds storage to reclaim space. use analyze for stats, optimize for fragmentation.. In practical terms, when to update statistics and when to rebuild. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Log files are critical to operations and can be a source of disk exhaustion if not managed. MySQL produces binary logs for replication and point-in-time recovery, the error log for server messages, the slow query log to find inefficient queries, and rarely the general query log which records everything. Each log type has a different purpose and retention requirement. For binary logs, set expire_logs_days to keep only the number of days you need for replication and recovery. For error and slow logs, use system-level rotation such as logrotate to rotate files and prevent growth. A safe retention strategy starts with identifying the recovery and replication needs: how many days of binary logs do you need to replay for point-in-time recovery, and do your slaves require older files? Then configure expire_logs_days and a rotation policy for the other logs. A common mistake is purging binary logs without checking slave replication positions; always verify slave status before deleting logs needed by replication. Automating log purges and rotation reduces human error and ensures logs do not silently fill disk space. Binary logs are essential for replication and point-in-time recovery, but if left unmanaged they grow indefinitely and risk filling disk. To manage them safely, first determine retention needs and the state of slaves. A safe manual purge example removes logs up to a named file or before a date. For example, PURGE BINARY LOGS TO 'mysql-bin.000123'; deletes all binary logs up to that file. Alternatively, PURGE BINARY LOGS BEFORE 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS'; removes older logs. Important safety checks: on each slave run SHOW SLAVE STATUS and note Master_Log_File and Exec_Master_Log_Pos to confirm they aren't behind the file you will remove. Another safe pattern is configuring expire_logs_days in my. cnf to let the server expire logs automatically. Automate purges only after confirming slaves and backups. A common misconception is that purging is harmless; purging logs used by a slave will break replication and may require expensive recovery. Error and slow query logs are valuable diagnostic tools but require rotation and regular inspection. The error log contains server-level messages such as startup errors, crashes, or plugin failures; check it periodically for recurring warnings that indicate emerging problems. The slow query log records queries that exceed a threshold; rotate it and inspect its contents to prioritize indexing or query refactoring. The general log captures all statements and is high overhead, so avoid enabling it in production except for short troubleshooting windows. Use system-level rotation tools like logrotate on Linux to archive and compress old logs and prevent growth. A practical pattern is to rotate logs daily and keep a short archive based on your operational needs. When you inspect logs, look for repeated patterns: the same error appearing frequently may point to a misconfiguration or failing job; repeated slow queries on particular tables indicate missing or poor indexes. A common misconception is to ignore slow logs because they grow quickly; instead automate rotation and use aggregated slow log summaries for periodic reviews. CHECK TABLE verifies a table's integrity and reports problems; REPAIR TABLE attempts to fix corrupted MyISAM tables. For InnoDB, corruption is much rarer thanks to crash recovery and transaction logs; if an InnoDB table is corrupted, the safest response is usually a full restore from backup. Use CHECK TABLE on MyISAM when you suspect corruption or after an improper shutdown, and follow with REPAIR TABLE if necessary. Example commands are simple: CHECK TABLE my_database. my_table; and REPAIR TABLE my_database. my_table;. However, REPAIR TABLE may not be effective for InnoDB and can risk data loss if run without a backup. A misconception is to run REPAIR TABLE on any error; instead, interpret CHECK TABLE output carefully and prefer restoring InnoDB data from backups. Also consider exporting data to a new table if repair attempts are risky. Always ensure a recent backup before running repair operations and, when possible, test repair steps in a staging environment. If you maintain mixed engines, prioritize migrating critical tables to InnoDB to leverage its crash recovery features. Security audits are routine checks of user accounts, privileges, authentication methods, and server configuration. Start by listing user accounts from mysql. user and inspect the grants for each account to ensure least privilege. Commands useful in this review include selecting user rows and SHOW GRANTS FOR 'user'@'host'; to see assigned privileges. Remove unused accounts and revoke privileges that are unnecessary. Also verify password strength and authentication plugins in use. A frequent misconception is to treat privileges as static; application needs change and privileges creep over time. Schedule regular reviews, and combine automated scans that report overly broad grants with human review before changes. When you remove an account or revoke privileges, ensure you log the change and test dependent applications in a staging environment if possible. Keep MySQL itself patched to reduce exposure to known vulnerabilities. Regular audits lower your exposure and make incident response simpler when an account is compromised. Automation ensures routine tasks run consistently and reduces human error. Two common automation methods are system cron jobs and MySQL's Event Scheduler. Use cron for shell scripts that can rotate logs, call mysql client to run commands, or manage backups. The Event Scheduler runs S Q L tasks inside MySQL itself and is convenient for database-only tasks. The chapter provides an Event example to purge binary logs daily: create an event that runs PURGE BINARY LOGS BEFORE (NOW() - INTERVAL 7 DAY) once per day. Remember to enable the scheduler with SET GLOBAL event_scheduler = ON; before creating events. When automating, include verification steps in scripts: check slave positions before purging binary logs, log actions and results to an audit table or file, and send alerts on failures. A misconception is to automate without retry and alerting; if a cron job silently fails you will miss critical maintenance. Test automation in a staging environment, and add safety checks that abort actions when preconditions are not met. Which maintenance task will you automate first and how will you verify its success?

These are the core concepts you should remember. First, routine maintenance is about predictable tasks that preserve performance, integrity, and security. Second, OPTIMIZE TABLE rebuilds data and reclaims space but is heavier and may lock tables, while ANALYZE TABLE refreshes optimizer statistics and is faster. Third, manage logs by purpose: keep binary logs long enough for replication and recovery, rotate error and slow logs to prevent disk exhaustion, and avoid prolonged use of the general log. Each concept links back to a safety practice: verify replication and backups before purging, schedule heavy operations during maintenance windows, and automate safe tasks with verification.
